newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish broad money growth on target-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Polish broad money growth on target-analysts.

text.p: A slowdown in the growth of money supply in Poland during November is in line with forecasts and makes the overall broad money growth target for this year plausible, analysts said on Wednesday.
The month-on-month rate of growth of broad money slowed to 1.4 percent in November after a 2.2 percent rise in October.

"The November money supply figures are all right. They show the real money supply growth target for this year of about five percent is likely to be met or only slightly exceeded," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, head analyst at the Planning Ministry.
Broad money grew by 23.63 billion zlotys since the start of the year. The central bank has envisaged a rise of 23 billion zlotys for the whole of 1996.
But analysts said the slightly higher growth was likely to be fully absorbed by demand for money which would eliminate any potential inflationary pressures.

"Last year the money supply growth target was 18 billion zlotys, money grew by 28 billion and yet inflation fell some eight points because the economy grew so fast that it absorbed the surplus," one analyst said.

Some analysts said an almost 90 percent credit rise for households since the start of the year, with only a 40 percent rise in deposits, was worrying because it signalled a weaker propensity to save and potential inflationary pressures.

But others said that consumer credit was growing from a very low starting point. In absolute terms, savings grew 15.44 billion zlotys in 11 months against a rise of just 5.04 billion zlotys in household credit.
"It is only the dynamics of credit growth which is so high, but the nominal figures are hardly any cause for concern," said Tomasz Bonecki-Duda of Creditanstalt Securities in Waarsaw.
Analysts also said that the fast credit growth fuelled domestic demand which, in turn, helped accelerate industrial growth after a slump in the first quarter of the year.
"This (the credit rise) winds up demand and despite the industrial slump in the first quarter production in 1996 is likely to end up higher than expected," said Chroscicki.
"The economy is going fine and does not need to be slowed down in any way by any sudden moves," he said.
The central bank has warned that fast credit growth was likely to translate into inflation next year and said that the bank would strive to keep real interest rates rising to curb lending growth.
